title: [The AI Logic] #25: "All my credentials are gone" (they weren't)
subtitle: Two n8n outages in six days, and the 36 GB one broken Gmail trigger wrote to disk.
body_html:
Hey,

The client said at the beginning that the credentials were totally broken in n8n, because they were not loading in the webpage, and the errors in n8n automations were telling that credentials were not working.

Same estate as issue #21, the 24,000 PLN maintenance quote.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY HAPPENING

I used Claude Code connected to the host, in this case the VPS where n8n is hosted, to investigate what is happening. I connected using an SSH connection as read only and asked Claude Code to investigate what is happening based on the symptoms.

Claude Code found out the usage of RAM memory, disk usage and CPU usage. Claude Code described that the disk is almost full. Then I realized that OK, there is no space for n8n to write down data. So I asked Claude Code to investigate what is filling the disk, and it narrowed it down to multiple files written by a specific n8n workflow. It was not one file but multiple files, and one trigger: the Gmail trigger.

The forensics:

  • 96 GB disk, 100% full, zero bytes free

  • 36 GB of it: the same email attachments, downloaded thousands of times over, around 32,000 writes in total

  • ~2,880 pointless downloads per day (~1.2 GB/day)

  • 27 of 35 failed executions that week traced back to the full disk, including 19 invoice runs in a row that nobody noticed

THE LOOP

It was a mistake from the person who did the original automation. The Gmail trigger node was set to download attachments, which were not used, and the workflow was not executed; just the node itself was executed, which was the trigger. It was happening in all workflows where the same trigger was used. It had a multiplying effect, because the same emails with attachments were downloaded thousands and thousands of times.

BEFORE FLIPPING THE SWITCH

Before removing downloading attachments, I reviewed the workflows that use the Gmail trigger with Claude Code, to validate that it will not break the automations’ business logic. Just after it I disabled attachments downloading.

THE “DELETED” CREDENTIALS

Freeing the disk fixed the issue, because n8n came back to normal operational mode. The credentials were not working properly because they were on the disk but not in the n8n runtime file, because it was not loaded on the reset, because n8n was not working correctly. So I restarted n8n and everything went working right.

WHY “JUST TURN ON RETENTION” WOULD NOT FIX IT

I wanted to make sure that the elements which are producing data will be under those retention configurations, to make sure that the disk will not be filled. Then I found out that it will not work. The Gmail trigger node generating files and storing them on disk is not under those retention policies, because they are just temp files. I needed to delete those manually and free up disk space.

IT HAPPENED AGAIN, FIVE DAYS LATER

This incident was because the first time I did not deep dive enough in understanding why the issue was happening. The first time I just freed up space on the disk.

This time I modified the workflow to not generate the data as it was generating. I tested it and made sure that it is working.

After both cleanup passes: 100% full down to 51%, about 47 GB free, 176,464 files removed.

WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS

Monitoring and prioritization of your workflows, to do proactive maintenance or react quickly for critical business automations.

This week: validate your hosting of n8n. If you have self-hosted, check what the usage of those machines is, to avoid critical crashes of n8n.

PICK OF THE WEEK

Claude Code, connected over read-only SSH. A good example of how we could use AI to help speed up investigations.

That’s it for this week.

Rimas

title: [The AI Logic] #24: nine studio photos of a shoe that never left the workshop
subtitle: A hand-painted sneaker, a printer in the background, and about five dollars of credits
body_html:
Hey,

I just saw a story on Facebook and decided to jump into it, to help make better images with AI. Anna paints custom artwork onto sneakers under the name MalovAna. This is the photo from her story.

The AI Logic is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

The original photo looked unprofessional and did not do justice to the effort put into painting the shoe. So, having proper studio photos, professional ones, will make the final product much better and emphasize the talent and art put on the shoe.

Same shoe. Same photo. Nothing was reshot.

HOW IT WAS DONE

The hardest part is to start and connect the right tools, which are the Higgsfield in this case, along with Claude Code skills or plugins. And do not be afraid to iterate over the items.

It ran in five stages. Each one takes the output of the last as its reference.

Stage 1. Clean the plate. One photo in, one usable image out.

Studio product photograph of this exact custom-painted white Nike Air Force 1 sneaker, isolated on a plain neutral light-grey seamless background. Remove ALL blue masking tape from the midsole, the collar and the tongue area. Remove the printer, cables, speaker, wall and every background object. Keep the hand-painted Pokemon artwork on the side panels exactly as it is: Pikachu on the toe box with yellow lightning-bolt background, Gengar in a purple circular badge in the middle panel, Charizard breathing fire across the heel panel. Keep the white leather midsole, white toe cap, white laces, white swoosh outline and the original silhouette unchanged. Perfect straight-on lateral profile, toe pointing left, shoe sitting flat, even soft studio lighting, soft contact shadow, sharp focus, high detail, clean commercial product photography.

Stage 2. Three test angles off that clean plate, to see whether the artwork survives a camera move.

Same custom-painted Pokemon Nike Air Force 1 sneaker as the reference image, identical shoe, identical artwork and colours. Rotate the camera to a three-quarter front view: toe pointing toward the lower-left, showing the toe box, the laces and the outer side panel with the Pikachu and Gengar artwork. Same plain neutral light-grey seamless studio background, same even soft lighting, same soft contact shadow, shoe sitting flat on the surface, sharp focus, clean commercial product photography, no text, no watermark.

Stage 3. One hero shot that fixes the set: the surface, the backdrop, the key light, the shadow. Everything after this copies it.

High-end studio product photograph of the exact custom hand-painted white low-top sneaker in the reference image. Hero three-quarter angle, shoe raised on a low matte concrete plinth, seamless warm light-grey studio backdrop with a soft luminous hot spot behind the shoe falling off to the corners, large softbox key from the upper left, subtle rim light separating the heel, soft contact shadow on the plinth. Reproduce the painted artwork exactly as in the reference: the yellow lightning panel at the toe, the purple circular badge mid-panel, the orange fire-breathing dragon across the heel, white leather midsole, white laces. Commercial footwear campaign photography, sharp detail, no text, no props.

Stage 4. Change only the camera. Four more angles, each carrying two references: the hero for the set, the clean plate for the artwork.

Studio product photograph of the exact custom hand-painted white low-top sneaker shown in the reference images. Match the lighting and set of the first reference exactly: same low matte concrete plinth, same seamless warm light-grey backdrop with a soft luminous hot spot, same softbox key from the upper left, same soft contact shadow. Change only the camera: three-quarter rear view, heel angled toward the lens, showing the heel counter and the orange fire-breathing dragon artwork wrapping around onto the side panel. Reproduce the painted artwork exactly as in the second reference. Commercial footwear campaign photography, sharp detail, no text, no props.

Stage 5. The specials: catalog profile on pure white for listings, a macro crop on the heel, a low angle on gloss black.

Clean e-commerce catalog product photograph of the exact custom hand-painted white low-top sneaker in the reference image. Perfect straight lateral profile, toe pointing left, shoe floating slightly with a soft drop shadow beneath it, pure white seamless background, flat even near-shadowless lighting so every detail of the painted panels is crisp. Reproduce the painted artwork exactly as in the reference. Shopify product listing photography, no text, no props.

Iterations with Higgsfield to get the outcome which I want.

WHAT SURPRISED ME

The interesting part is that the GPT Image 2 rejected generating images based on the real shoe because it represents the brand, which is Nike in this case. But in reality, I don’t want to use this brand or take it. I just want to put the real shoe in a nice environment.

The prompt that got refused named the brands:

Overhead flat-lay studio product photograph of this exact custom hand-painted Pokemon Nike Air Force 1 sneaker […] Preserve the artwork exactly: Pikachu with yellow lightning, Gengar in a purple badge, Charizard breathing fire.

The one that worked describes what is in the reference image instead:

Studio product photograph of the exact custom hand-painted white low-top sneaker shown in the reference images […] Reproduce the painted artwork exactly as in the second reference.

And also, the rendering of the 3D model did not work well, but over the iterations, I figured out how to do it. And the path forward was the Nano Banana Pro model, which worked well.

WHAT SHE WAS TOLD

I explained to the customer that those images were generated using AI from her original image. The majority of the pictures were generated from the side where the shoes were visible. So, we adjusted the accuracy.

THE NUMBERS

  • Credits spent, net of refunds: 102.75

  • In dollars, at the current top-up rate: about $5

  • Nano Banana Pro images: 13, at 2 credits each

  • Failed generations (Seedance twice, GPT Image 2 five times): refunded in full, 182 credits back

  • Average price of one product photo in Poland, 2026: 58.29 zł (kb.pl)

  • Nine shots at that rate: 525 zł

It took around one hour to generate all of those image iterations and communicate with the customer.

She was super amazed and happy with the outcome! I asked the customer to buy me a digital coffee on my page.

Do not be afraid that you need to pay for the tools, as the costs are very low compared to the outcome you are getting.

WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS

Visualizing your work in the right shape is very important. People form a first impression and take a look at it. Now, with the use of AI, you can have really nice-looking photos of real items without renting or buying a studio and hiring a professional photographer.

PICK OF THE WEEK

Go and try the Higgsfield. To generate their images and videos.

That’s it for this week.

Rimas

title: [The AI Logic] #23: They wanted a beautiful page. Nobody had written down the logic.
subtitle: Excel files, physical documents, and no way to react while the money was still moving.
body_html:
Hey,

I’m part of a business mentoring group. Someone there got to know me, we had a conversation about what we could do, and that is how this collaboration started.

The AI Logic is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

They build modular houses. They were tracking builds based on Excel files and physical documents, but there were no clear details and calculations online.

One spreadsheet per project, each one its own island. No view across builds, no history of who changed which number, and the margin recalculated by hand every time somebody needed it. A cost that arrived on paper in the office had to travel to a desk and into a sheet before it existed anywhere you could look at it.

WHY IT MATTERED

Their problem was that the company was not able to react to the costs and profit on each build-out phase.

The client was having builds where they lost money, or did not gain profit.

By the time the numbers were assembled, the phase they described was usually over. You can read a build that way. You cannot steer it. The decisions that protect a margin, swapping a supplier, catching a stage running long, renegotiating before the next order goes out, all have to happen while the build is still moving.

WHAT I DID FIRST, AND IT WASN’T CODE

It was a meeting, customer homework, and building the PRD document.

I was working with AI to do the PRD document, define use cases and what the scenarios are, and who will use the system.

The specification is important from a product perspective, because otherwise I would not be able to deliver in phases and early features delivery.

A PRD sounds like paperwork until you notice what it prevents. This one settled the questions that otherwise get answered by accident halfway through a build: what a project is, what counts as a cost, which stage it belongs to, who is allowed to see what, and what “finished” means for version one. The homework mattered as much as the meeting. The client knows their own process better than I ever will, and getting it out of their heads and onto a page is the part no model can do for you.

THE ARGUMENT I HAD TO WIN FIRST

The customer wanted to focus on everything in the system: graphical layout, design, beauty of the page.

But there are more important items to solve the customer problem, which is business logic, how the mechanics will look on the page.

I explained to the customer how it should be done, and that they will not benefit from a beautiful page if the business logic will not work, because they will not solve their problem.

Worth having that conversation early. A beautiful screen showing a number nobody trusts costs more than a plain screen showing the right one.

WHAT THE SYSTEM ACTUALLY DOES

The spreadsheets got replaced by one place where a build lives.

Cost entry follows the 15 construction stages the company already uses, so whoever enters an invoice works in the vocabulary they already speak on site. It runs on a phone, handles both VAT rates, remembers suppliers, and accepts past dates. That last one sounds trivial and isn’t: around 70 historical builds are being entered by hand with their real dates.

On top of that sits the calculation. Cost, income, profit and margin for each build, plus an overall margin across active builds, worked out the same way every time instead of by hand in a different sheet.

Every create, update and delete is written to an audit log. Who changed what, when. Six months later, when a number gets questioned, there is an answer.

A build is identified by its contract number. No names, no phone numbers, no email addresses, no uploaded documents. That keeps RODO out of the picture entirely, which is the cheapest kind of compliance there is: the personal data you never collect.

THE LINE THAT RUNS THROUGH THE DATABASE

One requirement shaped the architecture more than any other. The people who enter the costs are not shown profit, margin, or contract value.

That is easy to fake and hard to actually do. Hiding a number behind a button is decoration, because anyone who reaches the data another way can still read it. So the profit and loss figures come out of a single database function that checks who is asking and returns nothing where the answer is not theirs to have. Contract value is covered by the same rule, since margin is easy to reconstruct from contract value and costs.

The boundary holds at the layer a query lands on, not the layer a button lives on.

THE BUILD

I used Cursor AI, Vercel and Supabase for delivering the whole system.

Cursor, because it has the major models integrated in it. Web browser with design mode, auto mode for logic, and you can look into the files which it modifies. It is efficient.

Next.js and TypeScript on Vercel, Postgres and Auth on Supabase, with the conventions lifted from the client’s existing operations panel so the two systems feel like one product. Nothing exotic anywhere in it. The specification is what made it quick: with the decisions already written down, a working first version landed in a day, and every later phase had somewhere to attach.

The database was picked because all data needs to be collected even if you don’t know if you will use it. Later on you may need the data, but it would not be collected.

That choice costs almost nothing while you are still designing the schema and is close to impossible to fix afterwards. You cannot analyse a cost that was never recorded.

WHERE IT STANDS

The customer already started using it and is integrating the system day to day. I don’t have the data on where they are with the integration.

Whether it changed their numbers is too early to say, because the customer is integrating it now.

Payment reminders, statistics across projects and automated invoice import are specced and waiting. They were kept out of version one deliberately. The client’s actual problem was cost, profit and margin, and shipping that quickly was worth more than shipping all of it slowly.

WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS

Record and save what your business logic is in the specific field of your company. You don’t need to spend a lot of time, but build this habit of recording this logic.

This system was quick to build for one reason. The logic existed on a page before anyone opened an editor. AI coding tools are fast at producing what you can describe, and useless at guessing what you meant. The describing is the work. It stays yours regardless of which model you use next year.

Take action on what you are doing in your business that is not documented. Take any voice recording tool and start describing the item which is not documented.

PICK OF THE WEEK

GitHub Spec Kit is GitHub’s open-source toolkit for spec-driven development: you write the specification, and any AI coding agent builds from it. Install with uv tool install specify-cli, then run specify init my-project.

That’s it for this week.

Rimas
